video_title: Why BitMEX's Shutdown Got Nostalgia While Dead Tokens Get Rage: Uneasy Money
gist: Hosts Kane Wark and Taylor Monahan interview Offchain Labs CEO Stephen Goldfeder about the 2026 bear-market shutdown wave, arguing crypto has shifted from 'users buy your token' to hard revenue, and that L2 competition is now a proxy war between Robinhood chain (Arbitrum) and Base (Optimism) decided partly by licensing/business models. They dissect why BitMEX's shutdown produced nostalgia while tokenized shutdowns produce rage, a fresh wave of DPRK bridge hacks (Purpex/AFX misreported as an 'Arbitrum bridge' hack), Uniswap's permissioned pools with Securitize/Superstate as a move toward rights-bearing pseudo-equity tokens, Arbitrum DAO governance fixes, and Kyle Samani's public break with Multicoin over Hyperliquid.

themes.theme: Bear-market die-off: revenue replaces token price as the lifeline

insights.claim: Crypto project shutdown announcements are running at roughly ten a week less than six months into the 2026 bear market, far earlier in the cycle than in prior downturns, because it has become socially acceptable to capitulate rather than grind.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: An early, compressed capitulation wave means distressed acqui-hire and asset-purchase opportunities arrive sooner than the usual 18-24 month bear-market bottom playbook implies.
insights.quote: we're only like we're less than six months into this bare market, right? So, it's not like we're we're two years deep.

insights.claim: Founders shutting down in 2026 increasingly have live users but no monetization, meaning the failure mode is business-model failure rather than product failure.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder, co-founder/CEO Offchain Labs
insights.so_what: Screen portfolio and ecosystem projects on revenue per user, not TVL or DAU — usage metrics no longer predict survival.
insights.quote: it's like yeah we have users we just we just we don't make any money off

insights.claim: The old crypto business model was that users paid teams indirectly by buying the token, so token appreciation substituted for revenue; that channel is now closed and revenue has become a mandatory word.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark and Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: Reprice any token whose implicit cash flow was 'users buy the token' — that demand function is structurally broken, not cyclically weak.
insights.quote: whereas back in the day having users was sufficient for the token price like your users would buy the token that was how they paid you.

insights.claim: Crypto's cyclicality forces teams to compete unsustainably in bull markets, so companies that raised what would be a two-to-three-year Series A runway burn it in about one year and die.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: Underwrite crypto Series A burn at roughly 2-3x the equivalent SaaS rate when modelling default-dead dates for 2024-2025 vintage rounds.
insights.quote: teams that raised what would in a normal uh like ecosystem be like a three-year runway, right, in like a series A or something like that, like you know, two to three years burn through all their cash in like a year

insights.claim: Arbitrum and other ecosystems have shifted from grants toward a sustainable investment model, and Offchain Labs explicitly will not prop up products that are not working.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: Ecosystem-subsidy revenue lines in L2 app budgets should be marked down; grant-dependent projects face a funding cliff.
insights.quote: I don't think there's any like benefit in like propping up negative bad protocols.

insights.claim: Offchain Labs' grant test is that every dollar given out must have a credible story for two dollars returning to the Arbitrum ecosystem, in contrast to the logo-chasing model of paying everyone today and hoping they pay you next year.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: A concrete, reusable ROI filter for evaluating whether an L1/L2's incentive program is building durable share or just renting TVL.
insights.quote: for every dollar that we give out we should have a story of how $2 come back to the arbitrary ecosystem

insights.claim: Consolidation in crypto is coalescing around exactly two attributes — real distribution partners with real users (Coinbase, Robinhood) and solid technology — and the winners are those where the two combine.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: Use distribution-plus-tech as the survivorship screen for infrastructure bets; projects with neither are the shutdown candidates.
insights.quote: consolidation I would say around two things around uh solid distribution um that's like really really big whether it's Coinbase or Robin Hood but like real distribution partners with real users

themes.theme: L2 proxy wars: Robinhood chain vs Base, and licensing as the moat

insights.claim: Arbitrum and Optimism are no longer competing head-to-head as chains but through corporate proxies — Robinhood chain on the Arbitrum side and Base on the Optimism side — with the L2 teams supplying technology rather than fighting on the front lines.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: Value in the rollup stack accrues to whoever captures the distribution partner; track L2 competitive position by partner franchise, not by native chain TVL.
insights.quote: at the moment there's like a proxy war going on right between you know my old friends optimism and arbitrum u but it's not the chains themselves right it's these like giant behemoths

insights.claim: Offchain Labs' Business Source License, initially criticized, is now the core structural difference from Optimism because Coinbase and Base could choose to simply stop paying OP whereas large partners must contractually engage with Arbitrum.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: Licensing terms, not decentralization rhetoric, determine whether an L2 stack can monetize its biggest deployments — a durable revenue-capture differentiator to underwrite.
insights.quote: in Coinbase's case and bases case they were faced with the following decision. Should we continue to pay OP or should we just stop paying them?

insights.claim: Giving away open-source infrastructure for free without a licensing hook invites large capital-backed users to fork and cut the original team out, which the host frames as inviting capitalists into a communist utopia.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: For any open-source infra investment, ask what forces the largest deployer to keep paying; without it, revenue is voluntary.
insights.quote: Well, if you if you invite, you know, a bunch of capitalists into your communist utopia, like there might be some consequences to that potentially.

insights.claim: Arbitrum deliberately does not build first-party apps — no Arbitrum DEX, no first-party tokenized assets — so builders are not competing against the house, which Goldfeder frames as a structural differentiator versus other L2s.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: Neutrality at the app layer is a recruiting advantage for L2s; watch whether competitors that vertically integrate lose third-party builders.
insights.quote: we don't really get involved at the app layer. So you know you're not playing against us.

insights.claim: Offchain Labs runs a deliberate dual strategy in which Robinhood chain's success and Arbitrum One's own DeFi adoption are both top priorities, because relying purely on proxies is high-risk given proxies have their own agendas.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder and Kane Wark
insights.so_what: Concentration risk in the L2 business model: a partner defection would hit revenue, so monitor whether Arbitrum One's native DeFi activity holds independently.
insights.quote: Robin Hood chain success is like top of my list that I like want to ensure that but also equally top of my list is arbitration one success

insights.claim: Since Robinhood announced its chain, Offchain Labs has received a large and continuing volume of inbound business development from major Wall Street firms, which Goldfeder reads as evidence of a broader institutional trend.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: Leading indicator that more brokerages and TradFi institutions will launch their own chains — bullish for rollup-as-a-service revenue and for the stacks with enforceable licenses.
insights.quote: massive massive like Wall Street firms that we've gotten since then and continue to get

themes.theme: Why token failures draw rage and equity failures draw nostalgia

insights.claim: BitMEX's shutdown produced nostalgia rather than anger specifically because it never issued a token, so no retail spectators lost money on it despite almost every early trader using the platform.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: Community sentiment risk is a function of token issuance, not product quality — a real reputational cost to tokenizing that founders should price in.
insights.quote: It's sad that they're shutting down, but people aren't angry about it.

insights.claim: Token holders feel entitled to viciously post-mortem a failed token project even though a token holder's actual influence over a project is essentially identical to a customer's influence over BitMEX.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan, co-host
insights.so_what: The perceived governance rights of most tokens are illusory; this gap is exactly what rights-bearing token designs are trying to close.
insights.quote: the influence as a token holder or the influence you have over a token project versus Bitmax is essentially the same.

insights.claim: Because token projects are attention-driven and token purchases substitute for revenue, they tend either to become long-term zombies or to grind to zero and quietly shut the labs entity, so observers are often surprised the project was still alive.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: Distinguish zombie tokens (dead economics, live ticker) from operating businesses; zombie supply overhangs can persist for years before the formal wind-down.
insights.quote: token projects tend to be these like you know oftent times uh like things that either go long-term zombie right or like they burn through all their cash and then you just they kind of disappear they grind to zero

insights.claim: BitMEX was the consensus 2015 pick for a top-ten crypto company of 2030 — ahead of a then-nonexistent Binance — and it still failed, demonstrating that even maximal early advantage, revenue and tailwinds do not prevent startup failure in crypto.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: Base-rate discipline: incumbency and profitability in crypto exchanges are weak predictors of ten-year survival — size positions accordingly.
insights.quote: if you went back to 2015 and said like what are the startups that will be like the kings of crypto in in 2030, everyone would have said BitMX.

insights.claim: BitMEX's original model — no KYC, a Bitcoin-funded database with a troll box, treated as sufficiently decentralized because deposits were in Bitcoin — is unrepeatable today, as later attempts by Nat Alnaji showed.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: Regulatory arbitrage that created the last generation of exchange fortunes is closed; new entrants must underwrite compliance cost from day one.
insights.quote: being powered by Bitcoin was theme in 2014 is like sufficiently decentralized, right?

insights.claim: The irony of the rage asymmetry is that token projects were structurally far less sustainable than BitMEX, yet holders of tokens with no connection to revenue are the ones shocked when the project fails.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: Sentiment is not a signal of underlying business quality; the loudest post-mortems cluster on the weakest business models.
insights.quote: bro like you bought a token that had no connection to anything or revenues or anything and you're like shocked and appalled that like it didn't make it

themes.theme: Bridge hacks: DPRK crews, AI offense, and forgotten discipline

insights.claim: Four or five bridge hacks occurred in a recent short window with many more over the past month, reversing a multi-year period in which bridges felt safe and were no longer being drained daily.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan, co-host
insights.so_what: Cross-chain bridge TVL is being repriced for risk again; insurance costs and bridge-dependent yield strategies should be re-underwritten.
insights.quote: we had so many bridges and it's not even last week. I think there were four or five, but in the past month there have been many.

insights.claim: A widely circulated headline that 'the Arbitrum bridge has been hacked' was actually a third-party Purpex/AFX bridge only about a month and a half old, and Offchain Labs had to correct the narrative fast to avoid panic-driven secondary effects.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder and Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Automated hack-alert feeds and AI-written headlines create false attribution risk that can move sentiment on the wrong asset — a tradable mispricing window and a real operational risk for L2s.
insights.quote: we activated very quickly. Uh we uh confirmed that it wasn't the arbitrum bridge. We uh figured out whose bridge it was.

insights.claim: The Purpex/AFX bridge exploit involved five compromised hot validator signing keys and has been attributed to the same DPRK crew behind the LayerZero and Ronin hacks, who can extract keys even when they are split across separate servers.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan, co-host
insights.so_what: Multisig key-splitting across servers is not a sufficient control against this actor; bridges relying on hot validator signers are a persistent target class.
insights.quote: five five compromised hot validator signing keys.

insights.claim: AI has broken the human-versus-human security equilibrium that held bridge attackers at bay for roughly two to three years, and defenders have not yet marshaled equivalent tooling despite new open-source security agents and models now permitted to do cybersecurity work.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: Expect elevated exploit frequency until defensive AI tooling catches up — a window favoring shorter-duration and lower-TVL cross-chain exposure and favoring AI-security vendors.
insights.quote: we were able to like, you know, find an equilibrium where like the best humans were able to keep the other best humans at bay for a period of like 2 3 years.

insights.claim: Offchain Labs' historical bridge-risk mitigation was hardening the native bridge plus an education campaign pushing large exchanges off immediate sequencer-only confirmed withdrawals toward waiting for L1 finality or setting explicit size thresholds.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: A concrete operational control to check when assessing any exchange's L2 withdrawal policy — sequencer-only confirmation is an unhedged trust assumption.
insights.quote: initially actually many of the large exchanges were doing like immediate sequencer only confirmed withdrawals and we did a campaign that you should wait until it lands, you know, gets L1 finality

insights.claim: Offchain Labs does not audit third-party bridges deployed on Arbitrum and only performs second-level diligence on whether the team looks legitimate, so ecosystem bridge risk sits largely outside the L2's control.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: Do not treat an L2's endorsement or ecosystem listing as a security signal for a bridge; diligence must be done independently.
insights.quote: we don't audit their code but we try to check out are these like legitimate people

insights.claim: Demand for security is cyclical: in good times users only ask for features and the lowest fees, and only an FTX-scale event resets the appetite for decentralization and security guarantees.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: Security-differentiated infrastructure is structurally undervalued in bull markets and rerates after blowups — a repeatable timing pattern for infra positioning.
insights.quote: but like in good times times no one like hears about security which they just say like give me the features give me the lowest fees

insights.claim: The industry successfully beat 'don't roll your own crypto' into engineers but never established the equivalent norm against rolling your own bridge, even though a self-built bridge carrying enormous value is obviously absurd by real-world analogy.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: A cultural gap that predicts continued exploits — teams launching bespoke bridges rather than using vetted L2 bridge technology should carry a risk premium.
insights.quote: there was not yet this sentiment of like you can build your own bridge

themes.theme: Permissioned DeFi and the pseudo-equity token experiment

insights.claim: Uniswap Labs launched permissioned pools with Securitize, Superstate and Dalgo that embed the compliance check inside the V4 pool contract itself, letting tokenized-fund issuers restrict trading to approved investors without a centralized gatekeeper standing in front of the market.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: Moves tokenization's compliance layer from app to protocol, which is the missing plumbing for regulated assets to trade on public AMMs — watch adoption as the gating factor for RWA volume.
insights.quote: until now compliance for tokenized securities lived at the app layer. A gate standing in front of the market permission pools move those rules into the pool itself. that's the piece of plumbing tokenization has been missing.

insights.claim: Superstate's core thesis, per host and investor Kane Wark, is to replace rights-less tokens with instruments carrying some or all of the properties of equity — investor rights, disclosures, ties to revenue — with the unavoidable cost that fewer people are legally allowed to hold them.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host and Superstate investor
insights.so_what: If pseudo-equity tokens gain traction, rights-less governance tokens face a quality-competition problem they cannot answer without restructuring.
insights.quote: let's not have these um assets called tokens that have no rights um no obligations no uh you know ties to uh revenue

insights.claim: The host predicts Superstate will break out and that some big projects will choose the pseudo-equity token structure this cycle, producing the first real-time natural experiment on whether markets prefer rights with restrictions over open access without rights.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: A concrete, observable 2026 catalyst: track which large protocols adopt a rights-bearing structure and how their tokens trade versus rights-less comparables.
insights.quote: I think Superstate is going to uh like kind of break out and we'll see some big projects make this decision. So, we will get to see this experiment in real time.

insights.claim: The contrarian defense of permissioned DeFi is that controls are the precondition for rights: with literally no controls you get a free-for-all PvP market where holders have no rights, no upside claim and no information about what they bought.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: Reframes the compliance debate as a rights trade rather than an ideological loss — the argument that will be used to sell restricted instruments to crypto-native holders.
insights.quote: If there are literally no controls, if there's literally no nothing, you can't have either way. It's just a free-for-all. It's just PvP.

insights.claim: A definable segment of sophisticated capital — endowment-type investors — will not buy rights-less tokens and defaults to buying equity instead, meaning permissionless token design has an implicit ceiling on institutional participation.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: Rights-bearing structures are the mechanism to unlock a buyer pool currently absent from token markets — the marginal-buyer argument for tokenized equity.
insights.quote: if you are the Harvard endowment like go and buy equity in a thing if you're excited about it. Don't buy the magic beans that the guy's selling

insights.claim: Prevailing token designs — labs corp, foundation, DAO, token holder splits — were a function of the Gensler era and legal uncertainty rather than genuine preference, and are now being revisited as clarity improves.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: Expect a wave of token/entity restructurings as legal constraints loosen; current structures are not equilibrium designs.
insights.quote: a lot of the like token designs that were like popularized were very much a function of of the Gensler era

insights.claim: There was an incentive incompatibility in the prior regime where no individual team would take the legal risk of innovating on token structure, so everyone copied the same paved-path formula even without SEC blessing.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark and Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: Explains why token design stagnated and why a single credible first mover (e.g. Superstate) can unlock a rapid design shift.
insights.quote: there was like an incentive like incompatibility right where like no individual entity was going to take that risk.

insights.claim: Goldfeder expects the CLARITY legislation to function as a platform for rulemaking and deeper conversations about decentralization and ownership limits rather than instant answers, with real market effects a year or two after passage.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: Don't trade regulatory clarity as a near-term catalyst; the structural repricing from new token designs is a 2027-2028 story.
insights.quote: even if clarity passes tomorrow I think

insights.claim: Goldfeder would not trade Arbitrum's ~97% globally-eligible holder base for a 5% restricted base, because the censorship-resistance question is how easily a small, concentrated (largely New York-domiciled) holder set could be compelled to act.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: The strongest counterargument to pseudo-equity tokens for chains: broad distribution is a security property, not just a liquidity property.
insights.quote: how many people where are these, you know, where are these five doiciled and how easy would it be to compel the five to do something

insights.claim: Offchain Labs turned down seed investors in 2017-2018 who would only invest if Arbitrum issued a token; the token ultimately came from the need for governance over mutable contracts, with revenue routing to the token added later.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: Useful diligence lens: tokens created for governance necessity behave differently from tokens created to satisfy investors — check the origin story.
insights.quote: when we raised our uh seed round was 2017 2018 there were a few investors that said like hey um we'll only do it if you like do a token and back then I'm like I don't think arbitum needs a token I'm not doing a token

insights.claim: Chains are the main exception to the rights-less-token critique because they have core functionality that gives the token value without investor rights, whereas an application protocol like Compound would be a less controversial candidate for an equity-like instrument.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: Segment token exposure: app-layer tokens face the strongest pressure to restructure toward rights-bearing instruments; chain tokens least.
insights.quote: chains can actually have value uh you know without necessarily having investor rights attached to them because like they have like core functionality

themes.theme: Arbitrum DAO governance: apathy, delegates and the security council

insights.claim: Offchain Labs' self-identified early mistake was over-emphasizing decentralization by conflating the root of power with operational logistics, so the DAO ended up voting on trivia and smart delegates disengaged out of apathy.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: A reusable governance design principle — separate root-of-power decisions from operations — for evaluating whether a DAO can retain competent participants.
insights.quote: Like the DAO should not be voting what brand of toilet paper to use at the arbitrum.

insights.claim: Arbitrum's governance fixes were to eliminate professional delegate programs, put votes live on a fixed Thursday schedule so participants know when to look, and delegate operational decisions to the OpCo operating company via a vote.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: Concrete, copyable governance mechanics; also a signal of DAO maturation that reduces the tail risk of low-turnout capture.
insights.quote: So, what we did was we got rid of these professional delegate programs. We we uh put in a set of procedures where votes go live now on Thursday

insights.claim: Offchain Labs prohibits itself and its employees from voting their Arbitrum tokens directly in order to preserve space for community delegates.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: Materially changes the effective voting float in Arbitrum governance — relevant when modelling proposal outcomes or activist campaigns.
insights.quote: we for example on offchain don't allow uh ourselves or employees to directly vote uh with their tokens

insights.claim: The Arbitrum security council's intervention during the Kelp hack was, per Goldfeder, proof that a broadly elected external entity — not the founding team — can hold emergency upgrade power, with the token serving as the instrument that elects it.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: Distinguishes chains with tested emergency-response governance from those with untested multisigs — a differentiator in tail-risk pricing.
insights.quote: it was by design that there was this external entity right that's like you know broadly elected and it wasn't like me that had the power to do that

insights.claim: Governance apathy is an exploitable attack surface, as shown by roughly ten BarnBridge-style incidents where a vote passed unnoticed and the treasury was drained.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan and Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: Low-participation DAOs with sizable treasuries are a live risk category; monitor quorum ratios as a security metric.
insights.quote: that's the problem where sometimes just people aren't paying attention.

insights.claim: Delegating heavy power to an elected council works only when paired with an instantaneous recall mechanism that lets holders dissolve the council if it misbehaves, per Kane Wark's experience with Synthetix.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: Recall speed, not delegation depth, is the control that makes council governance safe — a diligence checkpoint for any DAO structure.
insights.quote: we had other checks where like you could vote them off instantaneously

themes.theme: Kyle Samani vs Multicoin and Solana's single-patron problem

insights.claim: Kyle Samani publicly told Solana builders that Multicoin, the firm he co-founded, is working against everything they are building — a rare public break by a founder against his own firm's ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: Signals a real rupture in Solana's most influential capital relationship; watch for follow-on shifts in Solana ecosystem funding.
insights.quote: if you're building in the Salana ecosystem, you should understand that multicoin is working against everything you're building.

insights.claim: The hosts believe Multicoin's large and now-profitable Hyperliquid position was the specific trigger for Samani's departure, because he viewed backing HYPE as a conflict with the firm's Solana commitment.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: Confirms crypto VCs are rotating capital from L1 ecosystem bets toward perp-DEX exposure, and that the rotation is contentious enough to break partnerships.
insights.quote: I think he was like you will you will invest in hype of my dead body and they were like goodbye.

insights.claim: Goldfeder argues contrarily that a Solana user worrying about which competing token a single VC also owns reveals a deeper ecosystem problem, and that Solana already proved after FTX that it is resilient to losing an over-propped patron.
insights.speaker: Stephen Goldfeder
insights.so_what: Downplays the fundamental impact of the Multicoin split on SOL; the tradable event is sentiment, not ecosystem viability.
insights.quote: I think we have bigger problems if I'm concerned about what a sing that a single VC is also invested in in a competing project

insights.claim: Solana's culturally homogeneous community repeatedly elevates a single patron figure — SBF as too big to fail, then Kyle Samani — a pattern the host contrasts with Ethereum's inability to agree on any leader.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark, host
insights.so_what: Concentration of narrative and capital in one figure is a recurring, unpriced tail risk in Solana's ecosystem structure.
insights.quote: SBF was like too big to fail for them and then they're like all right that didn't work out well how about Kamani

insights.claim: The host predicts Samani will launch his own fund, and finds the delay in doing so suspicious enough to suggest his exit from Multicoin had causes beyond the Hyperliquid disagreement.
insights.speaker: Kane Wark and Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: A new Samani-led fund would be a meaningful new source of Solana-aligned capital; the timing of the launch is the tell on the real reason for his departure.
insights.quote: My prediction is he will. My prediction is he will.
